scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire paper (Pfaff et al., BMC Medicine 2023) analyzes N3C electronic health record data on patients coded with ICD-10-CM U09.9 ('Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified'); Lyme disease is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This study used a large national EHR database (N3C, 16+ million patients, 34 health systems) to examine how the new ICD-10-CM code for long COVID (U09.9, available starting October 2021) was actually used in US clinical practice between October 2021 and May 2022, in a cohort of 33,782 coded patients. It reports which other diagnoses, procedures, and medications cluster with a U09.9 diagnosis, and shows that patients who received the U09.9 code were demographically skewed toward female, White, non-Hispanic individuals and toward lower-poverty, lower-unemployment areas compared to all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites. The authors argue this skew likely reflects disparities in who gets diagnosed and coded, not the true distribution of long COVID, and note that the code's nearly two-year delayed release left many earlier patients uncounted. The paper reports no direct medical costs, non-medical costs, lost income, or caregiving burden figures; its burden evidence is limited to diagnostic/coding patterns, care-utilization percentages, and demographic/SDoH disparities in who receives a diagnosis.

contextual_issues: The paper states the nearly 2-year delay in releasing U09.9 'potentially' left millions of long COVID patients uncoded, but gives no precise count - this is a hedged, unquantified estimate, not a modeled figure.
Treatment guidelines for long COVID are described as 'under development' at the time of writing (2023), implying care remains ad hoc, but no cost or utilization figure is attached to this gap.

The paper notes many long COVID symptoms are not captured in structured EHR fields and may only appear in free-text notes, implying further undercount of symptom burden beyond what diagnosis codes show.
Rehabilitation services (physical/occupational therapy) use is mentioned as rising with patient age, pointing to functional disability burden, but no percentage or cost is given.
Antibacterial medication use is noted as frequent across age groups with unclear clinical rationale (possible antibiotic overuse), but not quantified beyond being 'common.'
No caregiver time, lost income, travel cost, or direct/indirect financial burden is reported or quantified anywhere in the paper.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, non-medical cost (travel, paid help), or indirect cost (lost income, productivity, caregiving time) data are reported anywhere in this document; a cost-of-illness model cannot be built from it alone.

No chart-review-validated 'true' long COVID case count exists in this paper to assess the false-positive or false-negative rate of U09.9 coding, which the authors themselves flag as needed future work.
No national or population-representative prevalence estimate is given; findings are restricted to 34 of 76 N3C sites and cannot be generalized to a national diagnosed or estimated case count.

No sex/race/SDoH breakdown of the care-utilization or hospitalization percentages (e.g., 9.7% hospitalized, 22.8% imaging) is provided, limiting disparity analysis beyond the overall-cohort demographic composition reported in Table 1.

No outcome, cost, or longitudinal follow-up data beyond the 60-day post-index analysis window are reported, so this document cannot support any lifetime or multi-year burden projection without added assumptions.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool this paper's EHR/ICD-10-code-based N3C cohort (n=33,782, 34 health systems, Oct 2021-May 2022, HIPAA-limited EHR data) with the FAIR Health claims-data white paper's 25% hospitalization figure cited in the Results section - that figure comes from a different data source (insurance claims) and population, and the document does not adopt it as its own estimate, only contrasts it with its own 9.7% EHR-based figure.

Do not treat the demographic/SDoH comparison (U09.9 cohort vs. all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same 34 sites) as nationally representative; it is a site-specific EHR sample and SDoH variables are area-level (ZCTA) proxies, not individual-level measures.

Do not interpret the Louvain-algorithm diagnosis clusters (Fig. 2) as validated, causal 'subtypes' of long COVID - the authors explicitly describe them as hypothesis-generating co-occurrence patterns only, not diagnostic criteria.

Do not treat B94.8 ('Sequelae of other specified infectious and parasitic diseases') usage trends as a directly comparable measurement to U09.9 usage rates - B94.8 is a nonspecific placeholder code used for any post-infectious sequelae, not specific to long COVID, so uptake/rate comparisons between the two codes reflect different specificity and population capture, not the same underlying quantity at different time points.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The U09.9-coded cohort was significantly skewed toward female patients (66.9%) compared with all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same 34 N3C sites (55.6%; p<0.01); Table 1 also shows the female majority is present in every age stratum (57.0%-73.0%).

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The entire U09.9 cohort (n=33,782) is identified solely through an ICD-10-CM diagnosis/billing code recorded in EHR data (N3C). The paper itself reports that this EHR-coded cohort skews toward female, White, non-Hispanic patients and toward lower-poverty, lower-unemployment ZIP-code areas relative to all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites, and states that patients in more socially deprived areas 'may be less likely to receive a U09.9 code in a healthcare setting' despite those areas having higher COVID-19 case and death rates - directly illustrating access-driven undercounting independent of symptom-coding ambiguity.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The hospitalization-during-acute-infection percentage (9.7%), severe-hospitalization percentage (2.3%), and procedure-utilization percentages (e.g., 22.8% average imaging, 16.7%/7.4% average ECG/echo) are reported only as whole-cohort or age-stratified figures, with no breakdown by sex, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status.

contextual_issues: The paper states the nearly 2-year delay in releasing U09.9 'potentially' left millions of long COVID patients uncoded, but gives no precise count - this is a hedged, unquantified estimate, not a modeled figure.
Treatment guidelines for long COVID are described as 'under development' at the time of writing (2023), implying care remains ad hoc, but no cost or utilization figure is attached to this gap.

The paper notes many long COVID symptoms are not captured in structured EHR fields and may only appear in free-text notes, implying further undercount of symptom burden beyond what diagnosis codes show.
Rehabilitation services (physical/occupational therapy) use is mentioned as rising with patient age, pointing to functional disability burden, but no percentage or cost is given.
Antibacterial medication use is noted as frequent across age groups with unclear clinical rationale (possible antibiotic overuse), but not quantified beyond being 'common.'
No caregiver time, lost income, travel cost, or direct/indirect financial burden is reported or quantified anywhere in the paper.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, non-medical cost (travel, paid help), or indirect cost (lost income, productivity, caregiving time) data are reported anywhere in this document; a cost-of-illness model cannot be built from it alone.

No chart-review-validated 'true' long COVID case count exists in this paper to assess the false-positive or false-negative rate of U09.9 coding, which the authors themselves flag as needed future work.
No national or population-representative prevalence estimate is given; findings are restricted to 34 of 76 N3C sites and cannot be generalized to a national diagnosed or estimated case count.

No sex/race/SDoH breakdown of the care-utilization or hospitalization percentages (e.g., 9.7% hospitalized, 22.8% imaging) is provided, limiting disparity analysis beyond the overall-cohort demographic composition reported in Table 1.

No outcome, cost, or longitudinal follow-up data beyond the 60-day post-index analysis window are reported, so this document cannot support any lifetime or multi-year burden projection without added assumptions.

spec.title: Long COVID Diagnosis Code (U09.9) Uptake, Representation, and Care-Pattern Simulator
spec.boundary: This simulation reflects only diagnostic-coding patterns, demographic/area-level (ZIP-code) composition, and short-term (60-day) care-utilization percentages reported in one EHR-based study (N3C database, 34 US health systems, October 2021-May 2022, n=33,782 patients coded U09.9). It contains no direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, lost income, or caregiving-burden data and cannot support any financial burden estimate. Findings are not nationally representative, demographic/SDoH variables are ZIP-code-level proxies rather than individual-level measures, and the study does not establish a chart-reviewed 'true' long COVID case count.

takeaway.patient: This study looked at records from people who received the new long COVID diagnosis code (U09.9) in electronic health records between late 2021 and mid-2022. It found that the group of people who got this code was more often female and White than the overall group of people who had tested positive for COVID-19 at the same health systems, and more often lived in lower-poverty, lower-unemployment areas. Over a third of coded patients had no record of their earlier COVID-19 test in their chart, and about 1 in 10 had been hospitalized during that earlier infection. The study's authors suggest these patterns may reflect unevenness in who gets diagnosed and coded, not necessarily who actually has long COVID.
takeaway.care: Among patients coded U09.9 in this EHR cohort, about 9.7% had been hospitalized during their earlier acute COVID-19 infection, and roughly 22.8% received an imaging procedure within 60 days of the long COVID diagnosis, giving a rough benchmark for post-diagnosis workup intensity. The coded cohort was also demographically skewed (more female, more White, more concentrated in lower-poverty/lower-unemployment areas) relative to the full COVID-positive population at the same sites, and over a third of coded patients lacked a recorded index test for their earlier infection - suggesting documentation gaps that could affect how a care pathway identifies or tracks these patients.
takeaway.policy: In this 34-site EHR cohort, patients coded with the long COVID diagnosis (U09.9) were significantly more female (66.9% vs. 55.6% comparator, an 11.3 percentage-point gap) and more White (71.8% vs. 61.1%, a 10.7 percentage-point gap) than the overall SARS-CoV-2-positive population at the same sites, and were under-represented in higher-poverty, higher-unemployment, and higher-public-insurance-reliance ZIP code areas. The authors suggest this likely reflects disparities in diagnosis and coding access rather than the true distribution of long COVID. Any claims- or EHR-code-based prevalence or cost estimate built on U09.9 coding should be treated as an undercount, particularly in socially deprived areas.

patient: If you have ongoing symptoms after a COVID-19 infection but have not received a formal long COVID diagnosis, this study's findings suggest that diagnosis coding may not capture everyone with the condition equally - it may be worth raising persistent symptoms with a clinician even without a prior code.

If you were hospitalized or had a severe initial COVID-19 illness, you may want to ask a clinician what follow-up testing (such as imaging or heart-function tests) is typically considered for ongoing symptoms, since this study found these were common in the coded group.
Keep your own records of when you tested positive for or were diagnosed with COVID-19, since the study found many coded patients had no test date documented in their chart.
care: This finding about lower U09.9 coding rates in higher-poverty and higher-unemployment ZIP code areas may be worth checking against your own site's coding patterns to see whether similar gaps exist locally.

Benchmark your clinic's imaging and cardiac-testing (ECG/echocardiogram) ordering rates for post-COVID patients against this study's reported rates to see whether your pathway over- or under-utilizes these tests relative to this cohort.
Consider reviewing documentation practices for acute-infection test/index dates in patients ultimately coded U09.9, since over a third of this study's cohort lacked that record.
Review whether current U09.9 coding practices at your site are being applied consistently, given the study's note that clinicians have found coding guidance difficult to translate into practice.
policy: Flag claims- or EHR-code-based long COVID prevalence or cost estimates as likely undercounts in higher-poverty, higher-unemployment, and higher-public-insurance-reliance areas, based on this study's reported representation gaps.

Consider commissioning validation work comparing EHR/claims-coded long COVID counts against chart-reviewed or survey-based case identification, since this study does not establish a ground-truth prevalence figure.
Consider supporting clearer, more consistent coding guidance for U09.9 given this study's finding that clinicians have applied the code inconsistently since its release.

When evaluating long COVID treatment-guideline development, note this study's observation that guidelines remained under development at the time of its analysis, which may affect care variation independent of coding.

inputs.source: Results, p.4 (directly reported); 0-20 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the percent of the U09.9 cohort hospitalized during their earlier acute COVID-19 infection; it indicates how much of this coded long COVID population had a severe initial illness versus a milder course.

inputs.label: Percent of U09.9 cohort with imaging within 60 days of diagnosis
inputs.source: Discussion, p.8 (directly reported, averaged across age groups); 0-50 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the average share of U09.9-coded patients who received at least one imaging procedure within 60 days of diagnosis; it indicates how commonly imaging work-up accompanies a long COVID diagnosis in this cohort.

outputs.label: U09.9 cohort percent female minus comparator percent female (positive = more female representation among coded patients; negative = less)
outputs.interpretation: A positive value means the long COVID diagnosis code was applied to a larger share of women than their share among all COVID-positive patients at the same sites. The study reported an 11.3 percentage-point gap (66.9% vs. 55.6%, p<0.01), which the authors suggest may reflect disparities in who gets diagnosed and coded rather than the true sex distribution of long COVID.

outputs.label: U09.9 cohort percent White minus comparator percent White (positive = more White representation among coded patients; negative = less)
outputs.interpretation: A positive value means White patients made up a larger share of the coded long COVID cohort than of all COVID-positive patients at the same sites. The study reported a 10.7 percentage-point gap (71.8% vs. 61.1%, p<0.01), which the authors associate with diagnosis/coding disparities rather than a true difference in who develops long COVID.

outputs.label: Percent of U09.9 cohort with no recorded acute COVID-19 test
outputs.interpretation: This shows how much of the coded cohort's earlier infection is missing from structured EHR data. The study reported 37.2% (12,550 of 33,782 patients), indicating substantial gaps in what the record captures about patients' COVID history even after they receive a long COVID code.

outputs.label: Percent of U09.9 cohort hospitalized during acute COVID-19 infection
outputs.interpretation: This shows what share of the coded long COVID cohort had a hospitalized (more severe) initial COVID-19 illness. The study reported 9.7%, meaning most coded patients in this EHR cohort had a non-hospitalized initial infection.

outputs.label: Percent of U09.9 cohort with imaging within 60 days of diagnosis
outputs.interpretation: This shows how commonly imaging (e.g., chest X-ray or CT) was ordered shortly after a long COVID diagnosis. The study reported an average of 22.8% across age groups, which care teams can use as a rough benchmark for typical post-diagnosis workup intensity in this cohort.

scenarios.label: Demographics match overall COVID+ population
scenarios.goal: Shows whether equal demographic coding would close the reported representation gap.
scenarios.description: If the U09.9 cohort's sex and race composition matched the comparator cohort exactly, the representation gaps would be zero, illustrating the scale of the observed coding skew without implying a cause.

scenarios.label: Maximal demographic skew (stress test)
scenarios.goal: Tests how large the representation gap could appear under an assumed upper-bound skew.
scenarios.description: Using the input range's assumed upper bounds (80% female, 85% White) rather than any reported figure, this illustrates an extreme hypothetical skew scenario for comparison, not an observed finding.

scenarios.label: Cohort with sparse testing records and imaging
scenarios.goal: Illustrates how incomplete acute-phase documentation could coincide with limited follow-up imaging.
scenarios.description: Raises the share with no recorded acute test to the assumed upper bound (50%) and lowers imaging follow-up to the assumed lower bound (0%), illustrating a cohort with the least complete EHR capture described in the paper's documentation-gap caveats, as an association only.

scenarios.label: Cohort with thorough testing records and imaging
scenarios.goal: Illustrates the opposite case: well-captured testing and extensive follow-up imaging.
scenarios.description: Lowers the share with no recorded acute test to the assumed lower bound (20%) and raises imaging follow-up to the assumed upper bound (50%), illustrating a hypothetical cohort with the most complete EHR capture as a contrast case, not an observed subgroup.

package.documentation:
This simulator is built from Pfaff et al. (BMC Medicine, 2023), an analysis of the National COVID Cohort Collaborative (N3C) electronic health record database covering 34 US health systems. The cohort is 33,782 patients who received the ICD-10-CM diagnosis code U09.9 ('Post COVID-19 condition, unspecified') between October 2021, when the code was first released, and May 2022.

**Inputs** are the study's own reported percentages: the female and White shares of the U09.9-coded cohort, the matching shares among all SARS-CoV-2-positive patients at the same sites (used as comparison baselines), the share of the coded cohort with no recorded acute-infection test or index date, the share hospitalized during that earlier infection, and the average share receiving imaging within 60 days of diagnosis. All values are directly observed figures from the October 2021-May 2022 study period; none are dollar amounts, so no price year applies.

**Outputs** compute the sex and race representation gaps (coded-cohort percent minus comparator percent, in percentage points) and pass through the no-test, hospitalization, and imaging rates for direct reference.

**Limitations.** This EHR/ICD-10-code-based cohort reflects only who was diagnosed and coded, not the true distribution of long COVID. The study reports that the coded cohort skewed toward female, White, non-Hispanic patients and toward lower-poverty, lower-unemployment ZIP-code areas compared with all COVID-positive patients at the same sites, and states that patients in more socially deprived areas may be less likely to receive a U09.9 code despite those areas having higher COVID-19 case and death rates - so this figure should not be read as a complete count. The sex finding is notable beyond the pooled gap: a female majority appeared in every age stratum reported (57.0%-73.0%, Table 1).

The hospitalization and imaging-utilization percentages are reported only as whole-cohort or age-stratified figures, with no breakdown by sex, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroup; federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it.

Separately, the paper describes a systemic gap in the evidence/coding system: the U09.9 code was not released until nearly two years after patients began reporting long COVID symptoms, leaving many earlier patients uncoded, and clinicians have applied the code inconsistently in practice (one CDC Q&A attendee is quoted saying 'physicians don't speak coding'); treatment guidelines for long COVID were also described as still under development at the time of writing.

No direct medical cost, out-of-pocket cost, lost income, or caregiving-time data are reported anywhere in this document, so this simulator cannot support any financial burden estimate.

takeaway.care: Among patients coded U09.9 in this EHR cohort, about 9.7% had been hospitalized during their earlier acute COVID-19 infection, and roughly 22.8% received an imaging procedure within 60 days of the long COVID diagnosis, giving a rough benchmark for post-diagnosis workup intensity. The coded cohort was also demographically skewed (more female, more White, more concentrated in lower-poverty/lower-unemployment areas) relative to the full COVID-positive population at the same sites, and over a third of coded patients lacked a recorded index test for their earlier infection - suggesting documentation gaps that could affect how a care pathway identifies or tracks these patients.
takeaway.policy: In this 34-site EHR cohort, patients coded with the long COVID diagnosis (U09.9) were significantly more female (66.9% vs. 55.6% comparator, an 11.3 percentage-point gap) and more White (71.8% vs. 61.1%, a 10.7 percentage-point gap) than the overall SARS-CoV-2-positive population at the same sites, and were under-represented in higher-poverty, higher-unemployment, and higher-public-insurance-reliance ZIP code areas. The authors suggest this likely reflects disparities in diagnosis and coding access rather than the true distribution of long COVID. Any claims- or EHR-code-based prevalence or cost estimate built on U09.9 coding should be treated as an undercount, particularly in socially deprived areas.

patient: If you have ongoing symptoms after a COVID-19 infection but have not received a formal long COVID diagnosis, this study's findings suggest that diagnosis coding may not capture everyone with the condition equally - it may be worth raising persistent symptoms with a clinician even without a prior code.

If you were hospitalized or had a severe initial COVID-19 illness, you may want to ask a clinician what follow-up testing (such as imaging or heart-function tests) is typically considered for ongoing symptoms, since this study found these were common in the coded group.
Keep your own records of when you tested positive for or were diagnosed with COVID-19, since the study found many coded patients had no test date documented in their chart.
care: This finding about lower U09.9 coding rates in higher-poverty and higher-unemployment ZIP code areas may be worth checking against your own site's coding patterns to see whether similar gaps exist locally.

Benchmark your clinic's imaging and cardiac-testing (ECG/echocardiogram) ordering rates for post-COVID patients against this study's reported rates to see whether your pathway over- or under-utilizes these tests relative to this cohort.
Consider reviewing documentation practices for acute-infection test/index dates in patients ultimately coded U09.9, since over a third of this study's cohort lacked that record.
Review whether current U09.9 coding practices at your site are being applied consistently, given the study's note that clinicians have found coding guidance difficult to translate into practice.
policy: Flag claims- or EHR-code-based long COVID prevalence or cost estimates as likely undercounts in higher-poverty, higher-unemployment, and higher-public-insurance-reliance areas, based on this study's reported representation gaps.

Consider commissioning validation work comparing EHR/claims-coded long COVID counts against chart-reviewed or survey-based case identification, since this study does not establish a ground-truth prevalence figure.
Consider supporting clearer, more consistent coding guidance for U09.9 given this study's finding that clinicians have applied the code inconsistently since its release.

When evaluating long COVID treatment-guideline development, note this study's observation that guidelines remained under development at the time of its analysis, which may affect care variation independent of coding.

inputs.source: Results, p.5 (directly reported); 40-70 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source

outputs.label: U09.9 cohort percent female minus comparator percent female (positive = more female representation among coded patients; negative = less)
outputs.interpretation: A positive value means the long COVID diagnosis code was applied to a larger share of women than their share among all COVID-positive patients at the same sites. The study reported an 11.3 percentage-point gap (66.9% vs. 55.6%, p<0.01), which the authors suggest may reflect disparities in who gets diagnosed and coded rather than the true sex distribution of long COVID.

outputs.label: U09.9 cohort percent White minus comparator percent White (positive = more White representation among coded patients; negative = less)
outputs.interpretation: A positive value means White patients made up a larger share of the coded long COVID cohort than of all COVID-positive patients at the same sites. The study reported a 10.7 percentage-point gap (71.8% vs. 61.1%, p<0.01), which the authors associate with diagnosis/coding disparities rather than a true difference in who develops long COVID.

outputs.label: Percent of U09.9 cohort with no recorded acute COVID-19 test
outputs.interpretation: This shows how much of the coded cohort's earlier infection is missing from structured EHR data. The study reported 37.2% (12,550 of 33,782 patients), indicating substantial gaps in what the record captures about patients' COVID history even after they receive a long COVID code.

outputs.label: Percent of U09.9 cohort hospitalized during acute COVID-19 infection
outputs.interpretation: This shows what share of the coded long COVID cohort had a hospitalized (more severe) initial COVID-19 illness. The study reported 9.7%, meaning most coded patients in this EHR cohort had a non-hospitalized initial infection.

outputs.interpretation: This shows how commonly imaging (e.g., chest X-ray or CT) was ordered shortly after a long COVID diagnosis. The study reported an average of 22.8% across age groups, which care teams can use as a rough benchmark for typical post-diagnosis workup intensity in this cohort.

scenarios.label: Demographics match overall COVID+ population
scenarios.goal: Shows whether equal demographic coding would close the reported representation gap.
scenarios.description: If the U09.9 cohort's sex and race composition matched the comparator cohort exactly, the representation gaps would be zero, illustrating the scale of the observed coding skew without implying a cause.

scenarios.label: Maximal demographic skew (stress test)
scenarios.goal: Tests how large the representation gap could appear under an assumed upper-bound skew.
scenarios.description: Using the input range's assumed upper bounds (80% female, 85% White) rather than any reported figure, this illustrates an extreme hypothetical skew scenario for comparison, not an observed finding.

scenarios.label: Cohort with sparse testing records and imaging
scenarios.goal: Illustrates how incomplete acute-phase documentation could coincide with limited follow-up imaging.
scenarios.description: Raises the share with no recorded acute test to the assumed upper bound (50%) and lowers imaging follow-up to the assumed lower bound (0%), illustrating a cohort with the least complete EHR capture described in the paper's documentation-gap caveats, as an association only.

scenarios.label: Cohort with thorough testing records and imaging
scenarios.goal: Illustrates the opposite case: well-captured testing and extensive follow-up imaging.
scenarios.description: Lowers the share with no recorded acute test to the assumed lower bound (20%) and raises imaging follow-up to the assumed upper bound (50%), illustrating a hypothetical cohort with the most complete EHR capture as a contrast case, not an observed subgroup.
